fixes.explanation: Job says, "If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat." (Job 23:3) He's hurting, and his biggest wish is still to find God. I think that tells you where Job's heart is pointing. When life gets heavy, he wants to go to God's seat.
Job doesn't wish for anything about his friends in this verse. He says, "If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat." (Job 23:3) The one he's looking for is God.

Job doesn't say that here. He asks, "Would He contend with me in His great power?" and then answers, "No, He would certainly take note of me." (Job 23:6) What he says God would do is take note of him.
Forgotten isn't the word Job uses. He says an upright man could reason with God, and then "…I would be delivered forever from my Judge." (Job 23:7) Delivered is the word.
Job says, "when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold." (Job 23:10) He expects to come out as gold after God has tested him. That's a bold thing for a hurting man to say.
Dust is where I spent a lot of years, in the back of a junk drawer, so I know it well. It's not what Job says, though. He says, "…I will come forth as gold." (Job 23:10) Gold is the word he picked.
Job says no such thing. Here he talks about God. He says, "I have not departed from the command of His lips…" (Job 23:12) The command he's following is God's.
Job doesn't say he feels welcome. He says, "Therefore I am terrified in His presence; when I consider this, I fear Him." (Job 23:15) It's honest, and it's heavy.
Job says, "Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks." (Job 24:2) Moving boundary stones is the first wrong on his list. Stolen flocks come right behind it.

Idols aren't on Job's list here. He starts with this: "Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks." (Job 24:2) Moving boundary stones and pasturing stolen flocks are the wrongs he names first.
No tree shows up in this verse. Job says, "Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter." (Job 24:8) Mountain rain, rocks, and no shelter.
Job says the opposite. "They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry." (Job 24:10) He says the same about the winepresses: they tread them "…but go thirsty." (Job 24:11)
Job doesn't use a lion here. He says, "in the night he is like a thief." (Job 24:14) It's a heavy verse about killing the poor and needy, and the picture Job uses is a thief at night.

That's right. Job says, "In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light." (Job 24:16) The statement says they come out into the light like everyone else, and Job says the opposite. So the answer is False.

Job says, "their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards." (Job 24:18) Their land is cursed, and no one turns toward their vineyards. That's quite a picture next to "…foam on the surface of the water…"
Job doesn't call it fruitful. He says, "their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards." (Job 24:18) The word he uses is cursed.

Stolen isn't the word Job uses for their land here. He says, "their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards." (Job 24:18) Cursed is the word, and no one turns toward their vineyards.

Job says, "As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned." (Job 24:19) Drought and heat consuming melting snow is the picture he uses for Sheol stealing those who have sinned. Snow doesn't stand a chance against drought and heat.

That's not the comparison Job makes. He says, "As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned." (Job 24:19) The picture is melting snow consumed by drought and heat.

Job says the opposite. "He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways." (Job 24:23) God's eyes are on them, so they aren't hidden from Him at all. Job sets a sense of security right next to eyes that are watching.
